coccus-pseudomagnoliarum.summary: Citricola scale is a sap-feeding insect that can leave citrus foliage sticky with honeydew and darkened by sooty mold. Its appearance changes as it grows: young scales are flat and translucent beneath leaves, while mature females become oval, grayish bumps on twigs. Heavy populations can weaken trees and reduce fruit production. Ants, sticky leaves and black mold are useful clues, but checking the insects themselves matters because several other citrus pests leave the same signs.

sources.label: Citricola scale in citrus plantations in Croatia

zephyranthes-citrina.summary: Citron zephyrlily is a small bulb-forming perennial with bright yellow flowers held above a tuft of very narrow leaves. Each flower sits on a slender, upright stalk, giving the plant a light, grassy appearance between blooms. Native to parts of Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, it is also cultivated well beyond that range. A garden planting and a self-sustaining wild population are different situations, so location and evidence of seedlings are useful details when recording it.

sources.label: Kew: Zephyranthes citrina, descriptions and distribution

phyllosticta-citricarpa.summary: Citrus black spot is a fungal disease that marks citrus fruit with several kinds of blemishes, from tiny dark speckles to sunken spots with pale centers and dark borders. Severe infections can cause fruit to drop before harvest. The fungus can reproduce in infected fallen leaves, helping the disease persist around a tree. Because symptoms vary with the fruit's age and can resemble other problems, a photograph is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable confirmation.

sources.label: UF IFAS: A guide to citrus disease identification

aleurocanthus-woglumi.summary: Despite its name, citrus blackfly belongs to the whitefly family. Adults are dark and sooty-looking, and their young form conspicuous black, spiny patches beneath leaves. Feeding removes plant sap and produces honeydew, which can support a coating of sooty mold. Citrus is an important host, though many other woody plants can carry it. Natural enemies can keep populations low, so finding a few insects does not automatically mean a tree needs treatment.

xanthomonas-campestris.summary: The name on this record needs a closer check before it can support a citrus canker profile. Xanthomonas campestris is a recognized bacterial species, while older citrus literature used the more specific name Xanthomonas campestris pv. citri for the canker pathogen now placed in Xanthomonas citri. Dropping that final pathovar name changes the meaning. Resolving the original identification will help ensure that citrus symptoms and reporting advice are attached to the right organism.

sources.label: EPPO: Xanthomonas citri pv. citri datasheet

xanthomonas-citri.summary: Citrus canker is caused by a citrus-infecting pathovar of Xanthomonas citri, a bacterium that attacks leaves, shoots and fruit. Its raised, corky lesions often have a yellow halo and can make fruit unsaleable; severe disease also causes leaf and fruit drop. Wind-driven rain helps bacteria reach young tissue and wounds. Nursery plants can carry infection between places, including before clear symptoms appear, making careful diagnosis and plant-movement precautions especially important.

sources.label: UF IFAS: A guide to citrus disease identification

liberibacter-asiaticus.summary: Huanglongbing, often called citrus greening, is a serious citrus disease associated with the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. Infected trees may develop unevenly mottled leaves, yellow shoots and small, misshapen fruit that remain partly green. The Asian citrus psyllid carries the bacterium between trees, and infected propagation material can also spread it. Symptoms may take time to appear, so a healthy-looking tree is not proof of freedom from infection. Confirmed disease has no cure.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Citrus greening and Asian citrus psyllid

phyllocnistis-citrella.summary: Citrus leafminer leaves a delicate silver trail as its larvae tunnel just beneath the surface of new citrus leaves. The narrow, winding mine often contains a dark line of waste, and damaged leaves may curl around the developing insect. Young trees can lose valuable new growth, while established trees usually tolerate the injury. Feeding wounds can also make citrus canker infection easier where that disease occurs. The tiny adult moth is much less noticeable than its handiwork.

planococcus-citri.summary: Citrus mealybug looks like a small moving fleck of white cotton, often tucked into a leaf joint, fruit cluster or other sheltered spot. Beneath its waxy coating is an oval sap-feeding insect with short filaments around the body. It attacks many ornamentals as well as citrus, including plants grown indoors. Colonies can weaken growth and leave sticky honeydew that encourages sooty mold. New plants deserve a close inspection because small colonies are easy to overlook.

phyllocoptruta-oleivora.summary: Citrus rust mite is so small that the damage usually catches your eye before the animal does. Feeding on rind cells can leave oranges rusty brown and lemons silvery, changing the fruit's appearance. These pale, wedge-shaped mites also feed on leaves and green stems. In home gardens, light injury is often mainly cosmetic, but heavier infestations can matter in commercial production and may contribute to fruit drop. The similar pink citrus rust mite is a different species.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Citrus rust mite and pink citrus rust mite
UC IPM: Rust mite or silver mite

hediste-diadroma.summary: This clam worm lives out of sight in the mud of brackish estuaries, where its segmented body moves through a burrow. Native to the northwestern Pacific, Hediste diadroma has also been identified in estuaries on North America's Pacific coast. It gathers food from sediment and can filter suspended particles through a mucus net. Its resemblance to native worms makes casual sightings difficult to interpret, and the ecological effects of its introduction remain uncertain.

sources.label: Filter-feeding behavior of three Asian Hediste species

dysphania-pumilio.summary: Clammy goosefoot is a low, spreading herb whose small leaves and tiny flower clusters are easy to miss underfoot. Fine glandular hairs give it an aromatic, somewhat sticky character. The flowers sit close to the stems in the leaf axils, later producing minute dark seeds. Native to Australia, it has become established in other regions, often around disturbed or cultivated ground. Its modest appearance means close-up details are more useful than a distant photograph.

sources.label: Kew: Dysphania pumilio, Flora of Tropical East Africa account

heliotropium-amplexicaule.summary: Clasping heliotrope forms low, sprawling patches topped with curved clusters of blue-purple to pink flowers, each with a small yellow center. Its hairy, wavy-edged leaves sit close to the stems. This South American perennial can persist through a deep root system and regrow after its shoots die back. In introduced pasture settings it can compete with useful vegetation, and its toxicity to livestock makes a confirmed identification especially important around grazing land.

lepidium-perfoliatum.summary: Clasping pepperweed has an unusual contrast between its leaves: the lower ones are finely divided, while the upper ones are broad and wrap closely around the stem. Small yellow flowers appear above them, followed by little rounded seed pods. This short-lived mustard comes from Eurasia and is introduced in North America, where it often grows on dry, disturbed ground. Seeing both the lower foliage and the flowering stem makes identification much easier.

microthlaspi-perfoliatum.summary: Claspleaf pennycress is a small annual mustard with pale green foliage, tiny white flowers and flattened seed pods with a noticeable notch at the tip. Upper leaves clasp the stem, while lower leaves form a loose rosette. It occurs in dry, often lime-rich soils and can grow among crops and orchard vegetation. Botanical references may call it Microthlaspi perfoliatum, Thlaspi perfoliatum or Noccaea perfoliata, so matching the plant's features is more useful than relying on one name alone.

cotton-leaf-curl-gezira-virus.summary: Cotton leaf curl Gezira virus is a plant virus associated with leaf-curl disease in cotton and other members of the mallow family, including okra. Affected leaves may curl and develop thickened veins, but those changes are not unique to this virus. Reports from ornamental mallows have added another layer of uncertainty because findings in one host do not establish the same disease behavior in another. Reliable identification depends on a professional plant-health diagnosis.

sources.label: NVWA: Quick scan for cotton leaf curl Gezira virus, EPPO summary
Introduction of Cotton leaf curl Gezira virus into the United Arab Emirates

fallopia-dumetorum.summary: Climbing false buckwheat is an annual vine that threads its way through nearby vegetation with slender, twining stems. Its leaves are triangular to heart-shaped, and the small flowers are much less showy than those of a morning glory. As fruits develop, the surrounding flower parts form pale wings. Native across temperate Eurasia, it also occurs in disturbed North American habitats. It closely resembles native climbing false buckwheats, making mature fruit an important part of a useful record.

solanum-dulcamara.summary: Climbing nightshade scrambles through shrubs and fences, especially in moist places. Its purple flowers have petals that curve backward around a bright yellow center, and its berries ripen through several colors before turning glossy red. This perennial vine is native to Eurasia and has become established in North America, where it can spread through underground stems as well as seed. The attractive berries are not edible; all parts of the plant are toxic to people and domestic animals.

ficus-pumila.summary: Climbing fig can turn a wall into a dense covering of small, heart-shaped leaves. This woody evergreen vine, native to eastern Asia, attaches itself with short roots along its young stems. As it matures, it develops thicker branches with much larger, leathery leaves and may produce pear-shaped figs. That change can make the adult plant look surprisingly different from its familiar juvenile form. Its strong attachment to surfaces also deserves consideration wherever it is planted near buildings.

gonionemus-vertens.summary: Clinging jellyfish are small enough to overlook among seagrass and seaweed. Their transparent bells carry a conspicuous orange-brown cross, and sticky pads on the tentacles help them hold onto submerged vegetation. They occur in sheltered coastal waters such as bays, estuaries and ponds, rather than behaving like large jellies drifting conspicuously offshore. Contact can cause a painful sting, with reactions varying between people and populations. A clear photograph taken without touching the animal is the safest useful observation.

sources.label: Rhode Island DEM: Clinging jellyfish found in Point Judith Pond
Swedish Agency for Marine and Water Management: Jellyfish, clinging jellyfish section

cuscuta-epithymum.summary: Clover dodder makes a fine tangle of yellowish, red or purple threads over other plants, with tiny rounded clusters of flowers along its stems. It draws nourishment directly from its hosts, which include clovers, heather and gorse, rather than supporting itself with ordinary green leaves. Its role depends on the setting: it can trouble agricultural crops, yet it is also a native part of European heathland. The identity of both the dodder and its host helps explain a sighting.

sitona-hispidulus.summary: The clover weevil, also called clover root curculio, is a small mottled brown beetle associated with clover and alfalfa. Adults nibble small semicircular notches along leaf edges, but the more serious injury happens underground. Pale larvae feed on roots and can leave scars or deep gouges that weaken plants. A thinning patch of forage may therefore reflect damage that is not visible above ground, although disease and poor nutrition can produce similar symptoms.

sources.label: Utah State University: Clover root curculio

cotton-leafroll-dwarf-virus.summary: Cotton leafroll dwarf virus can be associated with curled or puckered leaves, distorted new growth and changes in the way cotton plants develop. Some affected plants become stunted, while others show elongated shoots with poor boll production. Symptoms vary with the cotton variety, growing conditions and the stage at which disease develops; some infected plants show little obvious change. Similar leaf distortion can result from insects or herbicide injury, so appearance alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

sources.label: Mississippi State Extension: Five things to know about cotton leafroll dwarf virus
Alabama Cooperative Extension: Cotton leafroll dwarf virus

begonia-cucullata.summary: Clubed begonia forms a soft mound of fleshy stems and glossy green leaves, with small white or pink flowers held above the foliage. The leaves have a wavy, finely toothed edge, and the seed capsules are unevenly winged. Native to South America, this begonia is grown ornamentally and has escaped cultivation in some warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States. Its many garden relatives and hybrids make a flowering, fruiting specimen more informative than a familiar garden name.

sources.label: UF IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Begonia cucullata

malva-verticillata.summary: Cluster mallow carries small pale flowers close to the stem, tucked into tight groups where the leaf stalks join it. Its broad, rounded leaves usually have shallow lobes and scalloped edges, giving a leafy plant a much larger presence than its flowers suggest. It has a long history of cultivation and also grows in fields, roadsides and disturbed ground. Several mallows look similar, and published records themselves sometimes reflect misidentification, so mature fruit is especially valuable for checking a sighting.

sources.label: Kew: Malva verticillata, Flora of Tropical East Africa account

trifolium-glomeratum.summary: Clustered clover is a small annual that spreads low over the ground or lifts its stems slightly above surrounding vegetation. Its pink to purplish flowers gather in tight, rounded heads nestled directly against the stem at the leaf joints. Each leaf has the familiar three leaflets, but the almost stalkless flower heads help distinguish it from more familiar garden and pasture clovers. Native around Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, it has also become naturalized elsewhere.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Trifolium glomeratum

rumex-conglomeratus.summary: Clustered dock is a slender perennial with branching upright stems and small flowers arranged in separated whorls. Many of those clusters have a little leaf beneath them, giving the flowering stem a more leafy appearance than some other docks. It grows in damp places as well as cultivated and pasture ground, and has been introduced well beyond its native Old World range. The modest flowers are easy to overlook, but the mature fruit coverings provide useful identification details.

sources.label: Kew: Rumex conglomeratus, Flora of Iraq account

erechtites-minimus.summary: Coastal burnweed is an upright, short-lived herb with narrow, regularly toothed leaves and clusters of small cylindrical flower heads. Unlike a showy daisy, its heads lack a ring of spreading ray petals. Botanists now commonly treat this plant as Senecio minimus, while Erechtites minimus remains a name used in older records. It occurs naturally in Australia and New Zealand, including moist forest settings, so its presence there should not automatically be interpreted as an alien invasion.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Senecio minimus

acacia-cyclops.summary: Coastal wattle is a dense shrub or small tree with narrow, leathery leaf-like structures and round golden flower heads. Its most striking feature appears when the pods open: each dark seed is surrounded by a fleshy orange to scarlet loop. Native to coastal Western Australia and South Australia, it has been planted elsewhere for shelter and dune stabilization. Outside its native range it can become invasive; South African conservation assessments identify it as a threat to sensitive coastal plant habitat.

tridax-procumbens.summary: Coatbuttons carries little daisy-like heads on long, wiry stalks above a low tangle of hairy stems and coarsely toothed leaves. A yellow center is bordered by just a few short white, cream or pale yellow rays, giving each head its button-like appearance. The plant is native to tropical America and is now widespread in warm regions elsewhere. It readily occupies bare and disturbed soil, where sprawling stems can form small patches between taller plants.

sources.label: Kew: Tridax procumbens, tropical flora descriptions
Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB: Tridax procumbens

nopalea-cochenillifera.summary: Cochineal cactus grows into a branching shrub or small tree, with flattened green pads and slender scarlet flowers. Despite its often nearly spineless appearance, the pads can carry tiny irritating bristles. Native to Mexico, it has been planted widely in warm regions and sometimes grows beyond cultivation. It also has a long history as a host for insects used to produce cochineal dye. Its presence in a garden is different from an established wild population, so records need that context.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Opuntia cochenillifera

solanum-capsicoides.summary: Cockroach berry is a prickly, short-lived member of the nightshade family, with broad leaves, white star-shaped flowers, and round fruits that turn orange-red. It grows in disturbed ground in warm, moist regions, including places outside its native tropical American range. The bright fruit can make it conspicuous along a roadside or neglected patch, but appearance alone is not a safe guide to edibility. Similar prickly nightshades have often been confused with it, making careful identification especially useful.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Solanum capsicoides

erythrina-crista-galli.summary: Cockspur coral tree brings clusters of vivid red, pea-shaped flowers to a branching shrub or small tree. Its leaves are divided into three leaflets, and the branches carry prickles. Native to South America, it is grown as an ornamental in warmer regions and has been introduced well beyond its original range.

colocasia-esculenta.summary: Taro is the plant behind a familiar tropical food crop and many garden elephant ears. Its large, heart- to arrow-shaped leaves rise from a thick underground corm. In warm wetlands, escaped plants can spread into dense patches along streams, ditches, and marshes, shading smaller vegetation. Pieces of the underground plant can help establish new patches when moved. Its value in cultivation and its ability to invade some waterways are both part of the story; the local setting matters.

cocos-nucifera.summary: Coconut palms are a familiar part of tropical coastlines, with a ringed trunk, long feather-like fronds, and large fibrous fruits. People have carried them widely for food, fiber, and useful materials. They also grow outside cultivation in suitable coastal habitats, where their ecological role depends on the place. Florida's assessment, for example, treats the palm differently across the state and identifies invasive behavior in the south with limited approved uses. A coconut record therefore needs more context than a garden label.

aspidiotus-destructor.summary: Coconut scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that can gather in pale, closely packed patches on leaves. Coconut and banana are familiar hosts, but it also feeds on many other tropical crops and ornamental plants. Heavy infestations yellow and weaken foliage. Young insects, called crawlers, move before settling beneath a protective covering; infested nursery plants can carry them to new places. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps help suppress populations, so visible scales do not automatically mean broad insecticide treatment is needed.

cydia-pomonella.summary: Codling moth is best known for the caterpillar that tunnels into an apple or pear and feeds around the seeds. Adults are small, mottled moths that blend into bark; the damage inside fruit is usually more noticeable than the moth itself. It also attacks walnuts and some other fruit crops. Several generations can develop during a growing season, depending on climate. Successful management combines watching for moth activity with timely fruit protection and removing infested fruit before more insects emerge.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Codling moth
Utah State Extension: Codling moth in Utah orchards

epilobium-hirsutum.summary: Hairy willow-herb is a tall perennial with fuzzy stems and pink-purple flowers, often growing where the soil stays moist. Introduced from Eurasia, it can form dense patches along wetlands, ditches, and stream edges in North America. Underground stems help a patch expand, while silky-haired seeds travel on the wind. Its flowers can be attractive, but a crowded stand can leave less room for other wetland plants. Native willow-herbs and fireweeds make careful identification worthwhile before any removal.

imperata-cylindrica.summary: Cogongrass is a spreading perennial grass that can turn varied vegetation into dense stands. Its extensive underground stems help it survive disturbance and move outward, while fluffy seeds and contaminated soil or equipment carry it farther. In the southeastern United States, it invades roadsides, pastures, and natural areas. The buildup of dry grass also increases fire danger and can change how habitats burn. Because a patch can regrow from underground pieces, controlling it usually takes a coordinated effort and repeated follow-up.

sources.label: Mississippi State Extension: Cogongrass identification and control

citrullus-colocynthis.summary: Colocynth, sometimes called bitter apple, is a trailing relative of watermelon adapted to dry landscapes. Its rough, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flowers spread close to the ground, followed by round fruits that change from mottled green to yellow. Unlike a sweet watermelon, the fruit has intensely bitter flesh. The plant is native across parts of Africa and Asia and adjacent regions. Its desert ecology is well documented, but a record outside that range does not alone establish local invasive damage.

sources.label: Kew: Citrullus colocynthis, regional flora descriptions

cuphea-carthagenensis.summary: Colombian waxweed is a small, branching herb with rough, hairy leaves and tiny purple to pink flowers. It can be easy to overlook among grasses in a damp, disturbed patch. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has become established in other warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. The flower's narrow tube and the plant's sticky hairs help distinguish it from superficially similar weeds. Its introduced presence alone does not tell us how strongly it affects a particular habitat.

agrostis-capillaris.summary: Colonial bentgrass, also called Rhode Island bentgrass, is a fine-leaved perennial introduced from Europe and nearby regions. Its airy flower clusters can give an unmown patch a soft haze. It has long been used in lawns, but also grows in fields, roadsides, and other open ground beyond cultivation. In some regions it becomes an invasive grass rather than staying a lawn plant. Separating it from related bentgrasses takes a closer look at the flowering branches and the small membranous flap where a leaf blade meets its sheath.

didemnum-perlucidum.summary: This colonial sea squirt forms thin living sheets over surfaces such as dock structures, ropes, rocks, and shellfish. Each sheet contains many tiny animals that filter food from the water. Colonies often look pale or marbled, but their appearance changes with conditions. It has spread through warm-water ports and can overgrow other organisms, creating concerns for aquaculture and some natural habitats. Its original home remains uncertain in parts of the scientific literature, even though introductions are documented in several regions.

symplegma-reptans.summary: Symplegma reptans is a colonial sea squirt that spreads as a low covering of many small animals joined within a shared outer layer. Native to the Indo-West Pacific, it has established in Southern California harbors, where it grows on docks, hulls, and other submerged surfaces. Colonies expand by producing new individuals through budding. At some sites they can cover large areas and compete for space with other attached organisms. Its resemblance to related sea squirts has complicated identification and some early records.

sources.label: Kawamura and Nakauchi: Development of buds in Symplegma reptans

tussilago-farfara.summary: Coltsfoot sends up yellow, dandelion-like flower heads before its broad leaves unfold. Later, the leaves form a low cover, with a pale, woolly underside that helps distinguish them from dandelions. Native across parts of Eurasia and North Africa, this perennial grows in moist disturbed ground and can spread into nearby habitats. Underground stems allow it to form persistent patches, while its fluffy seeds provide another route of dispersal. Removing only the visible leaves often leaves the living network below intact.

hyptis-pectinata.summary: Comb bushmint is a branching, aromatic herb whose tiny pale flowers line curved clusters like the teeth of a comb. It can grow tall enough to look like a small shrub, with toothed, hairy leaves and angular stems. Native to tropical America, it now occurs in other warm regions, often around disturbed ground, thickets, and moist edges. Although it appears in weed records, Florida's assessment does not document it as a problem species there. Its local behavior deserves attention without assuming severe impacts everywhere.

sources.label: Kew: Mesosphaerum pectinatum, regional flora descriptions

combretum-indicum.summary: Rangoon creeper is a woody climber best known for fragrant flowers that change from white through pink to red as they age. Hooks formed from leaf stalks help it climb over supports, and its broad leaves grow in opposite pairs. Its native range includes Tanzania and tropical and subtropical Asia through northern Australia. Widely cultivated in tropical gardens, it has also been introduced elsewhere. The mix of flower colors on a single vine makes it especially distinctive when in bloom.

asparagus-setaceus.summary: Common asparagus-fern looks soft and fern-like, but it is a flowering climber rather than a true fern. Its fine green sprays are familiar in houseplants and floral arrangements. Outside cultivation in warm regions, thorny shoots can climb through other vegetation, and birds carry seeds from its dark berries. Persistent underground growth makes established plants difficult to remove completely. Native to eastern and southern Africa, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere; Florida guidance recommends preventing escape and managing existing plants carefully.

melissa-officinalis.summary: Lemon balm is a perennial herb with wrinkled, toothed leaves that release a lemon scent when bruised. A member of the mint family, it produces small pale flowers visited by pollinators and has long been grown for kitchen and garden use. Native from the Mediterranean toward Central Asia, it has become established well beyond that range. Plants can spread and self-seed around gardens, so keeping an eye on seedlings is useful. Its familiar usefulness and occasional weedy behavior are both worth recognizing.

bambusa-vulgaris.summary: Common bamboo forms large clumps of tall, jointed canes topped by leafy branches. Native to parts of Asia and widely planted in warm regions, it supplies material for buildings, tools, and crafts as well as garden screens. It is a clumping bamboo, so its growth differs from the long-running bamboos familiar in some gardens. That distinction matters when evaluating a sighting or planning management. Florida's completed assessment for its southern region does not document an invasive problem there; other regions need their own assessment.
